transcript.text: Bosch SMS25AW00G, came back to E:09 on the display and the dishes are washed but stone cold. Is this an expensive fix?

It can be a moderately expensive repair rather than a small service item. On this Bosch dishwasher, E:09 means the flow-through heating circuit has failed or is not being recognised. With a stone-cold wash, the leading suspect is the heater built into the wash/circulation system; the temperature sensor or its wiring are the next possibilities. A control-board fault is possible, but less common. The cost varies mainly because the heater is often part of a larger circulation-pump/heater assembly, so parts and labour can make it a repair to price up rather than an inexpensive DIY fix. It is usually worth getting a fixed-price or written estimate before authorising work, particularly if the machine is older. 1. Confirm it is a true heating fault: after a completed normal or intensive cycle, carefully open the door. If there is no heat or steam and the water/dishes are genuinely cold, that supports the heater circuit rather than a drying setting.
2. Note whether the programme ran unusually long. A machine waiting unsuccessfully to reach temperature makes the heater/temperature-sensor circuit more likely.
3. Do not remove panels or attempt electrical tests unless you are confident and the dishwasher is switched off and unplugged. This fault normally needs access beneath/behind the appliance and is best diagnosed by an engineer, who can test the heater assembly, sensor and wiring before condemning the larger part. If the wash was cold throughout, I would arrange a dishwasher engineer and quote “Bosch E:09, no heat” when booking. If it was actually hot but only the dishes were wet, that would instead point to normal drying/rinse-aid/programme behaviour—but the E:09 code makes a heating-circuit fault the more likely explanation here.

Yes, the wash was cold throughout, the water was cold to touch mid-cycle and the dishes were cold. It's happened the last three runs and the cycle runs very long or stops. Machine is 9 years old so I'm weighing up repair vs replace. I do have a multimeter if a heater resistance check would help?

Yes — a resistance check would be useful, and could help decide whether an expensive heater/pump assembly is genuinely needed. E:09 means the flow-through heating circuit has failed or is not being recognised. The flow-through heater/circulation assembly is the leading suspect; the temperature sensor or its wiring remain possible if the heater itself tests sound. 1. Switch the dishwasher off at the socket and unplug it. Pull it out only if you can do so safely; turn off the water supply if moving it significantly, and have towels ready.
2. Only if you are confident removing the necessary external panel and identifying the heater connector: disconnect the appliance wiring plug from the heater terminals, then measure resistance directly across the heater terminals — never with it plugged in.
3. A healthy dishwasher heater commonly reads a low, finite resistance, often roughly 20–30 ohms. An open-circuit/OL reading strongly supports a failed heater assembly. A very low reading close to zero would also indicate a fault.
4. If it has a sensible finite reading, do not assume the assembly is good: the NTC temperature sensor, connector/wiring, or ultimately the control board could still be responsible. At that point an engineer diagnosis is more sensible than buying parts. Because this is normally an integrated flow-through heater rather than a simple exposed element, access can involve substantial dismantling underneath the machine. If you are not fully comfortable with the access, stop at this point and book an engineer quoting “Bosch E:09, cold wash throughout, long/stopping cycles.”

Ok, I'll give it a go with the machine unplugged and the panel off. Reading across the heater terminals on the pump is open circuit (OL). What does that mean for repair vs replace on a 9 year old machine?

[Heading: Likely cause: heater]
An OL reading means there is no continuous electrical path through the heater: it is open circuit. On this type of Bosch dishwasher, that commonly means replacing the circulation-pump/heater assembly rather than a small separate element. For repair versus replacement at nine years old: this is usually a borderline-but-reasonable repair only if the rest of the machine is in good condition and you can get a sensible fixed quote. It is not likely to be a cheap call-out repair, because the assembly and the labour to access and refit it are the main cost. If the quote is approaching roughly half the cost of a comparable new dishwasher, replacement is normally the better financial choice; if it is well below that and there are no leaks, noisy pump bearings, rack corrosion or other faults, repair can be worthwhile. The open-circuit result makes the NTC sensor, wiring and control board much less likely as the primary cause. An engineer should still inspect the connector for heat damage and confirm the diagnosis before fitting the assembly, but there is no good reason to spend money chasing the control board first. I cannot confirm an exact compatible assembly from the model reference alone, so use Bosch's official spares service or ask an engineer to identify it from the appliance's full E-number/FD information on the rating plate. When requesting a quote, give them: “Bosch dishwasher, E:09, wash remains cold, heater terminals test OL with appliance isolated.”
